answer: The default is already set: FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS = 0o644 in django/conf/global_settings.py.

The model `FilePathField` already handles a callable `path`. `formfield()` calls it with `self.path() if callable(self.path) else self.path`, and `deconstruct()` stores `self.path` unchanged. A callable therefore goes into the migration as a reference instead of a resolved string. The form field `forms.FilePathField` is not changed. It receives the already-resolved string.

The bug comes from the `ordering_parts` regex in `SQLCompiler`. Without `re.DOTALL`, `.` doesn't match newlines, so the search only captured the last line of a multiline `RawSQL`. That last line was then the key in the `seen` set, which made similar clauses look like duplicates. The current code already has the fix: the pattern is `^(.*)\s(?:ASC|DESC).*` compiled with `re.MULTILINE | re.DOTALL`, so `group(1)` now holds the full SQL before the ASC/DESC keyword. `get_order_by()` uses it at line 501 (`without_ordering = self.ordering_parts.search(sql)[1]`) to build the duplicate check. I didn't run anything to confirm the fix.

The fix is already in this codebase. `Media.merge` uses a `TopologicalSorter` over all the lists, so it no longer merges pairwise. It builds the dependency graph from every list first, then sorts it. It only warns with `MediaOrderConflictWarning` on a real cycle (`CycleError`). `Media.__add__` just collects the lists, and merging happens later over all of them.

The fix is already in the code. Both validators in `corpus/django/contrib/auth/validators.py` use `r"^[\w.@+-]+\Z"`. The trailing `$` has been replaced with `\Z`, so a trailing newline is rejected. The start anchor is still `^`, not `\A`. That makes no difference here, because `^` only matches at the start of the string unless `re.MULTILINE` is set, and these validators don't set it. The regex appears on line 10 (`ASCIIUsernameValidator`) and line 20 (`UnicodeUsernameValidator`). I only read the code and didn't run it.

The DurationField "invalid" error message in the codebase already uses the corrected format "[DD] [[HH:]MM:]ss[.uuuuuu]". It is the `default_error_messages` entry on `DurationField`. I found no copy of the old wrong format "[DD] [HH:[MM:]]ss[.uuuuuu]" anywhere in the files. I did not check whether the field now has a default help_text.

sqlmigrate sets self.output_transaction = migration.atomic and connection.features.can_rollback_ddl. This already matches the fix the ticket asks for. The BEGIN/COMMIT wrapper is only added when the migration is atomic and the database can roll back DDL.

The fast-delete path in `Collector.delete()` now clears the PK. After `delete_batch`, it runs `setattr(instance, model._meta.pk.attname, None)`, so a model with no dependencies gets its PK set to None after `.delete()`. I only read the code and didn't run anything to test it.

HttpResponse.make_bytes (called from the content setter) now treats memoryview like bytes: `if isinstance(value, (bytes, memoryview)): return bytes(value)`. The content setter also excludes memoryview from the iterable branch. So HttpResponse(memoryview(b"My Content")).content gives b'My Content'.

The migration's `update_proxy_model_permissions` moves permissions from the concrete model's content type to the proxy's content type. It does this with a bulk `.update(content_type=new_content_type)`. If permissions already exist for the proxy content type, which happens when a model is recreated as a proxy, the update hits the unique constraint on (content_type_id, codename). The current code wraps the update in `transaction.atomic` and catches `IntegrityError`. On a conflict it prints a warning and skips that model instead of crashing. The `try:` block starts at line 45.

The fix is already in this code. `iter_modules_and_files` in django/utils/autoreload.py special-cases `__main__` (and `__mp_main__`), which is usually manage.py. It has no usable `__spec__`, so the function falls back to `module.__file__` and adds it to the watched files. Without that branch, the `__spec__ is None` check skips the module, so manage.py is never watched.

The fix is in `iter_modules_and_files` in django/utils/autoreload.py. It wraps `path.exists()` in a `try/except ValueError`. When a network filesystem returns an embedded null byte in a path, it logs the error at debug level and skips that file (`continue`) instead of crashing.

This is already implemented. `LazySettings.__getattr__` in `django/conf/__init__.py` adds the SCRIPT_NAME prefix to `MEDIA_URL` and `STATIC_URL` when they are relative paths. It calls `_add_script_prefix`, which prepends `get_script_prefix()`. Absolute paths and full URLs (starting with `http://`, `https://` or `/`) are left unchanged. The prefixed value is cached in the settings object.

The models.E028 check is in `check_all_models`. It reports an error when several models share a `db_table`. When `settings.DATABASE_ROUTERS` is set, the same check is downgraded to the warning models.W035. The warning's hint tells you to verify that the models are routed to separate databases. Your setup, with different apps on different databases, should configure routers, which turns the error into a warning. Without routers, the error is still raised.

The fix is in `get_caller` in django/views/debug.py. It calls `resolve(request.path)` and catches `Http404`, which is broader than `Resolver404`. So an `Http404` raised from a path converter's `to_python` no longer causes a server error when DEBUG is True. The technical 404 response is built instead. I found this by reading the code and did not run it.

The check already exists. Field._check_choices in django/db/models/fields/__init__.py works out the longest string value in `choices`, including values in grouped choices. If that length is greater than `max_length`, it returns the error fields.E009: "'max_length' is too small to fit the longest value in 'choices' (%d characters)." The error is built at line 372.

EnumSerializer.serialize in django/db/migrations/serializer.py serializes enum members by name, as `module.EnumClass['NAME']`, instead of by value. The fix is already in this code. The line that builds that string is 144.

The two-digit year check is in `parse_http_date` in `corpus/django/utils/http.py`. It compares the year against the current year, not a hard-coded 70 cutoff. The check is `if year - (current_year % 100) > 50:` (line 121). A year more than 50 years ahead gets the previous century (line 124). Any other year gets the current century (line 126). The code in this repo already has this fix, so I made no changes.

The `__isnull` lookup already rejects non-boolean values. `IsNull.as_sql` raises `ValueError("The QuerySet value for an isnull lookup must be True or False.")` when `self.rhs` is not a `bool`. The check is in `as_sql`, so it fires when the SQL is compiled, not when the filter is built.

The fix is the `__str__` method on the `Choices` base class in `django/db/models/enums.py`. It returns `str(self.value)`, so a `TextChoices` or `IntegerChoices` member assigned to a model field now casts to its plain value (for example "first") instead of "MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE". `IntegerChoices` and `TextChoices` inherit this method. Field.contribute_to_class() used to set get_FOO_display unconditionally, so it replaced a user-defined override. The code here already has the fix. The autodetector's generate_altered_fields (django/db/migrations/autodetector.py) handles ForeignKey to_field renames: it repoints new_field.remote_field.field_name to the old field name when the target field was renamed (to_field_rename_key in self.renamed_fields).

The bug was in `Exact.get_prep_lookup` in `lookups.py`. When the right-hand side is a sliced `Query`, it used to clear the select clause and add `pk` every time. For `.values('m')`, that wiped the user's selected column. The query was then rebuilt with the default `pk` select, so `GROUP BY` came out as `U0."id"` instead of `U0."email"`.

This code already has the fix. Line 337 checks `if not self.rhs.has_select_fields:` before `clear_select_clause()` and `add_fields(["pk"])`. `set_values()` sets `has_select_fields = True` at `query.py:2387`, so a `.values()` queryset keeps its selected columns and its `GROUP BY`. The `In` lookup (`lookups.py:462`) has the same guard.

I only read the code and did not run the example, so I haven't confirmed that `b.query` now groups by `email`.

RegexPattern.match in corpus/django/urls/resolvers.py is where this is decided. The bug was that it filtered out the None kwargs before deciding whether to pass positional args. When the optional named group didn't match, kwargs became empty, so `match.groups()` was passed as positional args. With the pattern `(?P<format>(html|json|xml))?` that gave extra positional args, hence "3 were given". The fix is to decide args from the unfiltered `groupdict()` first. In that case, any named group means args is `()`. Only after that are the None-valued kwargs dropped. The code in the file already does it in this order (line 205 gets the groupdict, line 206 sets args, line 207 filters). The deciding line is 206.

The bug is in SQLite's `test_db_signature` in `corpus/django/db/backends/sqlite3/creation.py`. I didn't run the tests, and I didn't read the signature-grouping code in `django/test/utils.py` (`get_unique_databases_and_mirrors`) or `django/db/backends/base/creation.py`. The diagnosis rests on my recollection of the original upstream code.

The original signature only used the connection's `NAME` and added the alias for in-memory databases. For file-based test databases it left out `TEST["NAME"]`. With `default` and `other` both using the same `NAME`, their signatures were equal, so the test setup treated them as one database. Both aliases then opened the same file, which gives "database is locked".

The fix is the `else: sig.append(test_database_name)` branch at line 127. It adds the test database name to the signature, so each persistent file counts as a separate database. That branch is already in this checkout, so the repo appears to have the fix applied.

<parameter name="answer">SQLite DatabaseCreation.test_db_signature must include the test database name (TEST NAME) in the signature for non-in-memory DBs (the `else: sig.append(test_database_name)` branch); otherwise 'default' and 'other' persistent test DBs share the same signature and are treated as the same database, causing "database is locked".

The cause is in `find_ordering_name()` in `django/db/models/sql/compiler.py`. For `Child`, `pk` is the `parent_ptr` one-to-one relation. SafeExceptionReporterFilter.cleanse_setting() in corpus/django/views/debug.py. It only recursed into dicts, so values nested in lists or tuples were returned as-is. In this checkout it already has the fix: it now recurses into lists (line 136) and tuples (line 138) as well as dicts.

If any external column the subquery references is `possibly_multivalued`, it returns `[wrapper or self]`, so the whole subquery expression is grouped on. Otherwise it returns only the external columns. I read the code but did not run the example query.

The fast-delete guard is at line 473, with the counter update at line 474. The matching guard for regular deletes is at lines 507-508. I read the code but did not run it or any tests.

Query.check_filterable in django/db/models/sql/query.py checks `getattr(expression, "filterable", True)` on any RHS value, so a model instance with a `filterable=False` field is rejected as a non-filterable expression. The fix is the `hasattr(expression, "resolve_expression")` guard on the condition, so only real expressions are checked.

The check that skips applying the related model's default Meta.ordering is in find_ordering_name in corpus/django/db/models/sql/compiler.py, at line 1054: `getattr(field, "attname", None) != pieces[-1]`. It compares the field's attname (e.g. `root_id`) to the last piece of the ordering name. When you order by `record__root_id`, the last piece is `root_id`, so OneModel's `-id` default ordering is not applied. Ordering by `record__root_id` should therefore produce a single join and an ascending order.

I read the code but did not run the queryset. This source already contains the fix. Earlier Django versions compared the attname against the whole `name` (`record__root_id`), so it never matched. That mismatch would explain the extra self-join, the unexpected DESC from OneModel's `-id` ordering, and the flipped order for `-record__root_id`.

ValidationError.__eq__ is implemented in django/core/exceptions.py. It returns NotImplemented for non-ValidationError operands and otherwise compares hash(self) == hash(other). __hash__ uses (message, code, make_hashable(params)) for a single error and make_hashable(error_dict) for a dict. For a list it hashes the tuple of error_list sorted by message, so the order of errors in a list doesn't affect equality.

The fix is in `Query.set_empty()`, which `QuerySet.none()` calls. It adds a `NothingNode` to the outer query's `where`. It also calls `set_empty()` on every query in `combined_queries`. Before this, a union's outer query was marked empty but its sub-queries were not, so the combined SQL still returned all rows. Now each sub-query raises `EmptyResultSet` when compiled. In `get_combinator_sql`, a union omits empty parts, and an all-empty union raises `EmptyResultSet`.

This code is already present in the repo. I only read it and didn't run anything.

The crash is in `SessionBase.decode` in `corpus/django/contrib/sessions/backends/base.py`. The autodetector emits the AddIndex operations for a newly created model without making them depend on the `_order` field. That field only comes into existence when AlterOrderWithRespectTo runs. In `generate_created_models`, `related_dependencies` (lines 714-717) only lists the related fields and the model itself. The AddIndex calls at lines 718-726 use that list, so the optimizer can place AddIndex(['look', '_order']) before AlterOrderWithRespectTo, which is the ordering in your migration. The fix is to make those AddIndex operations depend on the AlterOrderWithRespectTo operation, or on `_order`, whenever `order_with_respect_to` is set. I haven't made that change or run anything.

Handling for `_order` dependencies already exists around lines 459-464. I only skimmed it and didn't confirm how it interacts with this case.

The fix is already in the code. ManagementUtility.execute() builds its CommandParser with prog=self.prog_name, so %(prog)s in the usage string uses the program name computed from the argv passed in, not sys.argv[0].

The crash comes from `exec(options["command"])` in `handle()` in `shell.py`. With no globals dict, code run by `exec` inside a method gets the function's locals. A `def` in that code then can't see names the same code imported, so `django` raises NameError. The fix is to pass a globals dict as the second argument. In this checkout that is already done: line 117 reads `exec(options["command"], globals())`. The stdin branch at line 127 is the same, with `exec(sys.stdin.read(), globals())`. I only read the code and did not run the failing example.

`globals()` here is the `shell.py` module's globals. The ticket suggested a fresh empty dict, and that would also fix the NameError. It would not leak the module's own names into the user's code.

The bug is in `KeyTransformIsNull` in `corpus/django/db/models/fields/json.py`. For `isnull=True`, `as_oracle` builds `(NOT <has-key> OR <lhs> IS NULL)`, and `as_sqlite` uses `JSON_TYPE(...) The crash comes from `Col.relabeled_clone()` in `django/db/models/expressions.py`. The `Expressions` DDL reference (`ddl_references.py`) calls `relabeled_clone()` when SQLite remakes the table and renames it. Without a guard, a `Col` with `alias=None` gets the new table name as its alias. The index SQL then renders as `"table"."col"`, and SQLite rejects the "." operator in index expressions. The guard at line 1157, `if self.alias is None: return self`, stops this. It is already in this checkout, so I could not reproduce the bug here. I did not run anything, so the guard is the likely fix location rather than a confirmed one.

The bug is in `MigrationRecorder.ensure_schema` in `django/db/migrations/recorder.py`. It creates the `django_migrations` table whenever `has_table()` is false. It never asks the database router whether `allow_migrate` permits the Migration model on that connection. `record_applied` and `record_unapplied` both call `ensure_schema()` first, so they also create the table on connections the router excludes. `applied_migrations` has the same gap, because it never checks the router either. The fix is to add a router check (`router.allow_migrate_model(self.connection.alias, self.Migration)`) in these recorder methods. I did not make or test that change.

The crash comes from how a SELECT column is compiled when its Q is always true. `~Q(pk__in=[])` resolves to a negated WhereNode. Its empty `pk__in` child makes `WhereNode.as_sql` raise `FullResultSet` (where.py:168), because a negated empty match means "match everything". `ExpressionWrapper.as_sql` passes that exception straight up. `SQLCompiler.get_select` handles it by compiling `Value(True)` in its place, which gives a valid expression instead of an empty one. The handler is the `except FullResultSet` branch at compiler.py:306-307. `Func.as_sql` has the same handling at expressions.py:975.

I did not run the query, and the `FullResultSet` handler in this copy of `get_select` looks like the fix already. The empty `SELECT AS "foo"` output from the ticket probably predates it.

EnumSerializer.serialize in django/db/migrations/serializer.py now handles combined Enum flags. For an enum.Flag value, it gets the member list: `list(self.value)` on Python 3.11+, otherwise `enum._decompose(enum_class, self.value)` reversed. It then emits each member as `module.Class['NAME']` and joins them with " | ". A plain Enum still serializes as a single member.

The IndexError comes from `if str_number[0] == "-":` in `format()` in django/utils/numberformat.py. When the number is None or an empty string, `str(number)` gives an empty string or "None", and indexing `[0]` on an empty string raises IndexError. The fix is to use `str_number.startswith("-")` instead of indexing, or to return early for empty values.

The squash handling is in `CreateModel.reduce()` in `corpus/django/db/migrations/operations/models.py`. The `elif isinstance(operation, RenameIndex) and operation.old_fields:` branch (lines 344-370) handles the `index_together` to `indexes` transition. When a `RenameIndex` has `old_fields`, it removes those fields from the `index_together` option. If `index_together` ends up empty, it drops the option. It then adds an equivalent `models.Index(fields=operation.old_fields, name=operation.new_name)` to `indexes`. The squashed `CreateModel` therefore no longer uses `index_together`, so the deprecation warning goes away.

The select mask for `only()` is built in `Query._get_only_select_mask` (`corpus/django/db/models/sql/query.py`). I couldn't find a defect in this corpus, because the code already contains the fix. The mask key for a reverse relation must be the concrete field (`field.field`), not the reverse relation object. This is the check that does it (line 784, with the key assignment on the lines after it):

```python
if field in opts.related_objects:
    field_key = field.field
```

The compiler looks the mask up with that same field, `select_mask.get(related_field)` at `compiler.py:1253`, where `related_field` is `o.field`. If the mask were keyed by the reverse relation object instead, that lookup would find nothing and return `{}`. An empty mask means every column of the related model is selected, which matches the 4.2.1 query in the report.

I checked the other places that read or build the mask, and none of them looked wrong:
- `_get_defer_select_mask`
- `get_default_columns`
- `select_related_descend`
- the rest of `get_related_selections`
